source.title: Transformer verbatim in-context retrieval across time and scale
source.authors: Kristijan Armeni; Marko Pranjic; Senja Pollak

page_placements.theme: Verbatim in-context retrieval as short-term or episodic memory (behavioural)

record.tranche_reason: Measures the training trajectory of verbatim in-context retrieval with a repeated-noun loss-change measure, conceptually testing the sudden behavioral retrieval transition. It does not measure induction heads or the training loss curve.
record.gate_note: The study measures repeated-noun retrieval behavior, not attention-head formation. It reports zero-shot benchmark correlations and noun-concreteness and list-position effects; these do not directly test the listed induction-head claims.
record.test_reason: It tracks a behavioural proxy for induction (verbatim copying of repeated nouns) across Pythia training checkpoints. It asks whether this follows Olsson et al.'s early sudden transition. It does not identify heads, measure in-context loss by token index, or track the training-loss bump. So it bears only on the timing and abruptness part of V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that verbatim retrieval of repeated nouns develops in a sudden transition early in training (about 1% of tokens) across 14M–12B, slightly later for the two smallest, and stays stable. They find it correlates with zero-shot benchmark learning. A concrete-noun advantage near the transition dissipates later except in the smallest models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses repeated noun lists and a loss-change measure to assess behavioral retrieval, extending that paradigm across Pythia training checkpoints and sizes. It does not detect or intervene on induction heads, measure loss by token index, or track the training loss curve.
record.method_sensitivity: The smallest two model sizes plateau later than larger models. Retrieval also varies with noun position and noun concreteness.

fits_no_version.finding: Around the retrieval transition, concrete nouns show 7–17% greater repeat-loss change than abstract nouns. By the end of training the advantage is small (2–6%) and remains only in the three smallest models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-training verbatim in-context retrieval is transiently stronger for concrete than abstract nouns.

fits_no_version.finding: Retrieval is stronger for later list positions; for 70M it rises from 62% on the first noun to 95% on the last.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verbatim retrieval strengthens over successive repeated items.

fits_no_version.finding: The trajectory of copying ability correlates with zero-shot benchmark trajectories (ρ≈0.95 on four tasks for 12B). The correlations are unstable for WSC, LogiQA and ARC-challenge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning of verbatim copying tracks learning of some zero-shot benchmarks.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning (CoNLL), 2024
record.problems: The study measures output behavior rather than internal mechanisms, so it cannot establish induction-head formation. It uses one vignette, English only, and a single training corpus/setup; the authors identify the vignette and language coverage as limitations.

untested.parts: Induction-head formation itself, the coincident training-loss bump, and any in-context-learning score (loss falling with token index) aligned with the transition.
All of it: no previous-token heads, composition analysis or attention analysis.
All of it: no per-token-index in-context-learning measure and no attribution to heads.
All of it at the head level. Copying behaviour is shown across Pythia sizes only, with a single family, corpus and run.
All of it: training data and setup are not varied.
All of it: copying is not contrasted with few-shot task learning through mechanisms.
All of it: no sub-step or internal decomposition of formation.

missing.what: Benchmark-correlation results for Pythia 160M–6.9B; correlations and their reliability grow with model size.

record.verdict_notes: The study measures output behaviour only. The authors explicitly leave internal mechanisms to future work and merely compare their timing to Olsson et al. (1–2B vs 2.5–5B tokens). The V2 verdicts therefore rest on a behavioural proxy for induction and should be weighted accordingly.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not identify previous-token heads, test head composition, or analyze induction-head mechanisms.
It tests the timing of behavioral verbatim retrieval, but not induction-head formation or a bump in the training loss curve.
It does not measure loss falling with token index in large models or test whether induction heads carry most in-context learning.
It evaluates behavioral retrieval in Pythia models at several sizes, but does not identify induction-behavior heads or test other model families, architectures, modalities, or training runs.
It uses Pythia models trained on the Pile and does not vary training data or setup to test their effects. Noun semantics are varied as an evaluation condition, not as a training-data condition.
It does not compare repeated-token retrieval with few-shot task learning or test other mechanisms as the main carrier of few-shot learning.
It measures behavioral retrieval trajectories, not separate internal formation steps or overlapping transitions among heads.

rows.subject: Pythia suite (8 tested sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Measured repeat loss change when the second list contained nouns unrelated to the original list.

conditions.value: 230 vignettes with no matching in-context nouns to retrieve

rows.value: Overall remained below 10%; the authors report no important loss change.
rows.note: The text reports this control across the experiment without giving per-model values.
rows.check: This is a control (unrelated nouns in the second list) that validates the measure. It is not itself a result on V2, so it should not be linked to V2.

rows.subject: Pythia models (14M to 12B)
rows.stage_stated: around the retrieval transition during training
rows.operation_detail: Compared repeat loss change for concrete and abstract noun lists.

conditions.value: around the transition point, approximately 1–2B tokens

rows.measure: Difference in mean repeat loss change, concrete minus abstract
rows.value: Concrete nouns showed 7–17% greater change; the advantage occurred in all models.
rows.note: This is an evaluation-stimulus semantic effect, not a test of training-data dependence.

rows.subject: Pythia 14M, 31M, and 70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared repeat loss change for concrete and abstract noun lists.
rows.measure: Relative loss-change advantage for concrete nouns
rows.value: Concrete-noun relative loss change was 2% to 6% greater on average.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals shown for the plotted results
rows.note: The authors characterize the end-of-training advantage in these three smallest models as detectable but small.

rows.subject: Pythia models (all tested sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Measured repeat loss change separately by noun position in the three-item list.

conditions.value: first versus later items in the list

rows.measure: Repeat loss change by noun position
rows.value: Retrieval improved for items later in the list in all models; figure-only for the general comparison.
rows.note: The authors state that the position advantage was more pronounced for 14M, 31M, and 70M models.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Measured repeat loss change separately by noun position in the three-item list.
rows.measure: Repeat loss change by noun position
rows.value: 62% for the first token and 95% for the last token.
rows.note: The authors give this as an example of the later-position advantage.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, paragraph discussing position-specific retrieval; Figure 2b.

rows.subject: Pythia 12B
rows.operation_detail: Correlated the retrieval learning trajectory with zero-shot benchmark learning trajectories.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between repeat loss change and benchmark accuracy across checkpoints
rows.value: ρ ≃ 0.95 on the four tasks, as reported collectively.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence interval; N = 5000 bootstrap samples
rows.note: The study also says most tasks generally showed positive correlations; estimates were less stable for Winograd schema challenge, LogiQA, and ARC (challenge).

source_check.problem: The collective approximation matches Section 4.2, but Figure 4 lists a different task selection and individual coefficients.

relationships.condition: Pythia 70M–12B, behavioural copying of repeated nouns
relationships.reason: Repeat-loss change rises after about 1B tokens and plateaus by about 4B tokens (under 5% of training), near 100% (R3–R8). This is consistent with an abrupt early transition, though heads and the loss bump are not measured.
relationships.display_finding: Repeat-loss change rose after about 1 billion tokens and plateaued near 100% by about 4 billion tokens, within 5% of training.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Pythia 70M–12B, behavioural copying of repeated nouns
source_check.reason: R3–R8 show an early behavioural rise after about 1B tokens and plateau at approximately 4B. Support is confined to behavioural retrieval; head formation and the training-loss bump are untested.

relationships.reason: Onset is similar, but the curve is slower and plateaus only after about 20B tokens at about 80%, so the transition is less narrow in the smallest models (R1–R2).
relationships.display_finding: Retrieval improvement began at similar times but plateaued only after about 20 billion tokens, at approximately 80% repeat-loss change.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R1–R2 show slower behavioural learning, plateauing after roughly 20B tokens with final repeat-loss change around 80%, qualifying the narrow-transition component.
